description.value: The study examined mind wandering capacity in behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia, Alzheimer's disease, and healthy controls, and related performance to gray matter integrity and resting-state functional connectivity.

value: We predicted that both of these groups would show an overall reduced propensity for mind wandering relative to controls.
Given that environmentally dependent behaviors are characteristic of the bvFTD syndrome, we further predicted an increase in stimulus-bound forms of thought in bvFTD.

description.value: The study included bvFTD, AD, and healthy control groups; participants provided informed consent and were assessed with a thought-sampling task and neuroimaging.

value: Reduced gray matter intensity in the striatum, anterior-mid thalamus, orbitofrontal and insular cortices, left hippocampus and parahippocampal gyrus, and left posterior insula was associated with lower mind wandering index scores, reflecting a tendency toward stimulus-bound thought.
These findings underscore the role of hippocampal and parahippocampal regions, as well as regions overlapping the default, limbic, and salience networks, in supporting mind wandering.

value: In controls, the tendency to mind wander was positively associated with left posterior cingulate cortex-left posterior hippocampus connectivity and negatively associated with left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex-left hippocampal formation and left posterior cingulate cortex-ventromedial prefrontal cortex connectivity.
In AD and bvFTD, the association between left posterior cingulate cortex-left posterior hippocampus connectivity and mind wandering was negative, opposite to the control pattern.

bvFTD showed additional associations between mind wandering and connectivity involving the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, hippocampal formation, posterior cingulate cortex, anteromedial prefrontal cortex, and hippocampal regions, suggesting altered or compensatory functional architecture.
